messages.subject: Re: naturally truncated distances
parts:
> > I'm working on my Master's project doing density estimates of cavity nestings birds with the line transect methods. Transects are placed in forest stands that are delineated by GIS. The stands very in size and shape and are in one of 4 strata based on cover type and size classes. I'm working in an area in which forest stands are often surrounded by expanses of grassland (Blue Mts. NE Oregon). Therefore, outside of the stand is nonhabitat for cavity nesters and detections are impossible beyond the boundaries of the stand. My question is how this situation will turn out in the analysis. For example, in large stands where the distance on either side of my transect in which I can detect a woodpecker is unlimited, the detection function for some of these species is quite great. However, in some of these narrow stands where I can see the edge as close as 50 m away, the ability to detect the same birds is only as great as that distance. I've been trying to lay transects
!
pe!
> > rpendicular to these edges. Is this the right solution? Should the data be treated differently when the distance from the transect to the edge is close? You can send a reply to me personally at :nssa...@yahoo.com or to the whole group if you prefer. I only have access to email about once a week. Thanks for any advice.Nicole Seaman

This issue is discussed on pp214-6 of the 2001 distance sampling book (see
the RUWPA web page below for info - click on 'publications'). It will be
discussed in greater detail in the advanced volume, which is due to go to
the publishers soon. A simple solution to the problem is to define a grid
of lines over the survey area, where the survey area has a 'bufferzone'
extending a distance w beyond the habitat, where w is the maximum
detection distance from the line. Then survey the line segments in the
bufferzone as well as those in the trees. With random placement of the
grid of lines (and sufficient lines - say 15 or more), this ensures a
uniform distribution of objects with respect to distance from the line.
Thus the short detection distances recorded from lines running through
small patches of trees are offset by relatively large distances recorded
from lines passing close to, but outside, patches of trees.
